Financial data is naturally ordered through time.
A time series approach helps us answer questions like:

Is there a long-term trend?
Is the series becoming more unstable?

Are recent observations unusual?

Simple idea: Time series analysis helps us understand how a pattern changes before, during, and after an important event.

text:
What Is a Time Series?


A time series is simply a list of measurements collected one after another over time.
What makes it special — the order of rows matters. Monday connects to Tuesday. You cannot shuffle the data like a survey without losing information.
Two ingredients every time series needs:



📅

Timestamp When was it measured? (date, hour…)



📏

Value What was recorded at that time?



💡 Our example: Stock market daily returns, 2018–2022. The COVID shock creates a clear “before and after” — perfect for learning every concept.

title: placeholder
text:
Two Key Concepts: Trend & Volatility

📈 Trend — the Big-Picture Direction
The trend is the overall direction of the series — ignoring the day-to-day noise. Found by taking a rolling mean (average of the last N days).










The navy line removes the noise — now the up → crash → recover story is obvious.

📊 Volatility — How Wild Is It?
Volatility = standard deviation of daily changes. High volatility means the series is jumping around a lot. Low = calm and predictable.










⚡ COVID made the market 4× more volatile — risk jumped overnight.

title: placeholder
section: Two More Concepts: Stationarity & Structural Break
text:
Two More Concepts: Stationarity & Structural Break

🔄 Stationarity — Does It Stay Consistent?
A series is stationary when its average and spread stay roughly the same over time. Most analysis tools need this.
The raw price keeps rising forever → not stationary. The daily % change bounces around zero → stationary.









💥 Structural Break — When Everything Changes
A structural break is a point where the series permanently changes its behaviour. Models trained before the break will fail after it.










Volatility before COVID: ~0.8%/day. After COVID: ~1.4%/day. Old models stopped working. This is a structural break.

title: placeholder
text:
Anomaly Detection — Spotting the Unusual
An anomaly is a data point so far from normal that it deserves attention. We use the simple 3-sigma rule — flag anything more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.



The Rule Flag a point if:   |value − mean|  >  3 × std dev In normal data only 0.3% of days would be flagged. So when the rule fires — something genuinely unusual happened.






















⚡ During the shock, ~9% of days were anomalies — 30× the normal rate. The algorithm found the crisis automatically, using only mean and std dev.

title: placeholder
text:
Summary — 5 Things to Remember



01 Time Series = Data in Order


A time series is measurements over time — and order matters. Monday connects to Tuesday. Shuffle the rows and you destroy the information.




02 Trend = Long-Run Direction


Smooth out the noise with a rolling mean to reveal whether the series is going up, down, or sideways. COVID shows a clear crash then recovery.




03 Volatility = How Wild It Is


Standard deviation of daily changes measures how much the series jumps around. COVID pushed volatility 4× above normal — visible instantly in a rolling volatility chart.




04 Structural Break = Permanent Change


When the series changes behaviour and stays changed, that is a structural break. COVID doubled market volatility permanently. Models built on old data fail.




05 Anomaly Detection = Spot the Unusual


The 3-sigma rule flags anything more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. No labels needed — the data finds its own extreme events automatically.




THE BIG IDEA


These tools work on any data over time — temperature, sales, hospital admissions, energy use. COVID and the stock market are just our learning example.

What Is Time Series Analysis?



📊 What It Studies

Data ordered through time — each observation linked to a specific date or period. Examples: stock prices, returns, inflation, sales, exchange rates, website traffic.



🎯 Main Goal

Identify patterns, changes, and unusual behavior — then translate those into actionable decisions.



🔑 Key Questions



Is this series trending?


Did behavior change at a specific date?


Are recent values unusually extreme?





🏦 Why Finance?

Risk is not constant. Asset prices evolve through time. Static analysis misses all of this.



Core idea: A number without a timestamp is just a number. Time series analysis turns timestamps into insight.

Concept 1: Volatility



📐 Definition

The standard deviation of returns over a rolling window. Measures how much prices fluctuate around their average.



⚠️ High Vol Means



Larger gains and losses


More uncertain forecasts


Higher risk premiums


Harder to hedge





🏦 Who Uses It

Banks (VaR models), hedge funds (position sizing), regulators (systemic risk), options traders (implied vol).



📏 How We Measure

30-day rolling window standard deviation of daily returns. The standard for short-term market risk monitoring.

Concept 2: Structural Break




📖 Definition


A structural break occurs when the statistical properties of a time series — its mean, variance, or relationships — change permanently at a specific point in time.


After a break, models fitted on pre-break data give poor forecasts and misleading risk estimates.




🔬 Detection: Chow Test


Formally tests whether regression coefficients are the same before and after a hypothesised break date. Applied to COVID: the null hypothesis of “no break in March 2020” is overwhelmingly rejected.






⚡ COVID-19 as a Structural Break



Volatility jumped from 0.8% → 3.5%/day


Asset correlations changed dramatically


Investor behavior shifted to panic mode


Market expectations re-priced entirely


Government policy became a key price driver


Pre-COVID risk models failed immediately

Why This Matters for Business



🏦 Banks & Risk Managers

Recalibrate Value-at-Risk models after vol spikes. Pre-COVID models dramatically underestimated tail risk during the shock.



📈 Investors

Rebalance using rolling volatility as a signal. High-vol regimes call for defensive allocations and hedging strategies.



🏭 CFOs & Firms

Plan working capital around elevated uncertainty. Structural breaks can persist months before markets normalise.



🔍 Analysts

Anomaly detection as an early-warning system. Flagging 3-sigma events gives decision-makers critical lead time.



Core message: Market analytics is not only about predicting prices — it is about measuring, monitoring, and communicating risk in a constantly changing world.

title: Understanding Market Shocks Through Time Series Analysis
text:
Key Takeaways



01 Returns Over Prices


Log returns are stationary, comparable, and risk-revealing. Always analyse returns for financial time series — never raw price levels.




02 Volatility = Risk


The 4× spike in rolling volatility during COVID is the clearest, most actionable signal in the data. Volatility regimes are real and measurable.




03 Structural Breaks Are Real


COVID-19 created a genuine regime change. Models trained on pre-crisis data failed immediately. Detecting the break date is step one.




04 Simple Rules Work


A 3-sigma anomaly rule flagged ~79% of extreme events in only 8% of the time window. Powerful signals don’t always require complex models.

title: Understanding Market Shocks Through Time Series Analysis
text:
Final Conclusion


COVID-19 showed that markets can shift quickly and completely during major events. Time series analysis gives us the tools to see those shifts clearly, measure them precisely, and respond intelligently.


By studying returns rather than prices, measuring rolling volatility, identifying structural breaks, and flagging anomalies — analysts gain a real decision-making edge.

Multinomial Logit (MNL)
The MNL model estimates utility values for each course.

choice_tasks = []

for (rid, task), grp in choices.groupby(
    ['Record ID','Task']
):

    offered = grp['Item'].tolist()

    chosen = grp.loc[
        grp['Response'] == 1,
        'Item'
    ].values[0]

    choice_tasks.append({
        'offered': offered,
        'chosen': chosen
    })



Log Likelihood Function

def neg_log_likelihood(beta_free):

    beta = np.concatenate(([0], beta_free))

    ll = 0

    for obs in choice_tasks:

        offered = [i-1 for i in obs['offered']]

        chosen = obs['chosen'] - 1

        utilities = beta[offered]

        denom = logsumexp(utilities)

        chosen_utility = beta[chosen]

        ll += chosen_utility - denom

    return -ll



Estimate MNL Model

initial = np.zeros(K-1)

result = minimize(
    neg_log_likelihood,
    initial,
    method='BFGS'
)

beta_hat = np.concatenate(([0], result.x))

Discussion
Despite using different assumptions and algorithms, the six methods converge strongly on the same top drivers:

Top drivers (ranked 1–3 across methods): Trustworthy, Good Service, and Positive Impact
Weaker drivers (ranked 7–9): Differentiates, Popular, and Build Quality

Why methods can disagree:

Pearson r ignores multicollinearity and inflates the apparent importance of correlated attributes.
Standardized β penalises correlated predictors heavily — a variable may get a near-zero coefficient even if it is substantively important.
Shapley values and Johnson’s Relative Weights distribute shared variance fairly across correlated predictors, making them the most theoretically principled linear methods.
Random Forest Gini additionally captures non-linear relationships and attribute interactions.

The convergence of five independent methods on the same top three drivers gives strong confidence that trust, service, and positive impact are genuine priority areas for improving customer satisfaction.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Card and Krueger (1994) examine the effect of a minimum wage increase on employment in the fast-food industry. In April 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour, while neighboring Pennsylvania’s minimum wage remained unchanged at $4.25. This policy discontinuity provides a natural experiment well-suited to a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework.
The identifying assumption is that, absent the policy change, employment trends in New Jersey fast-food restaurants would have evolved similarly to those in Pennsylvania. Under this parallel trends assumption, the DiD estimator isolates the causal effect of the minimum wage increase on employment.
In this replication, the goal is to reproduce the paper’s central finding: the increase in the minimum wage did not reduce employment in fast-food restaurants.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Conclusion
This replication closely matches the findings of Card and Krueger (1994). Across multiple specifications, including simple difference-in-means, OLS with robust standard errors, and a controlled regression with chain and ownership indicators, the estimated effect of New Jersey’s minimum wage increase on fast-food employment is positive and inconsistent with the prediction that higher minimum wages necessarily reduce employment.
The result survives a robustness check that excludes permanently closed stores, and the distributional evidence confirms that the finding is not driven by outliers.
More broadly, this exercise demonstrates how Difference-in-Differences can be applied to evaluate real-world policy changes, and how standard econometric tools (regression, robust inference, and sensitivity analysis) strengthen causal claims beyond simple comparisons of means.

text:
Introduction
Blueprinty is a software company that develops tools specifically designed to help engineering firms prepare and submit patent applications to the U.S. Patent Office. Their marketing team would like to make a strong claim: firms using Blueprinty’s software appear to receive more approved patents than firms that do not.
At first glance, this sounds like a straightforward comparison. If Blueprinty customers receive more patents on average, perhaps the software is helping firms prepare stronger patent applications. The challenge, however, is that Blueprinty’s customers are not selected at random. Firms choose whether to purchase the software, and those decisions may themselves be related to patenting success.
For example, older firms may have larger R&D budgets and more established legal departments. Certain regions may also contain more innovative firms or stronger engineering ecosystems. If Blueprinty customers systematically differ from non-customers in these ways, then a simple comparison of average patent counts could incorrectly attribute those differences to the software itself.
Ideally, we would observe firms before and after adopting Blueprinty’s software, allowing us to estimate how patent outcomes changed over time. Unfortunately, no such panel dataset is available.
Instead, Blueprinty collected data on 1,500 mature engineering firms. For each firm, the dataset includes the number of patents awarded over the last five years, the firm’s regional location, the firm’s age since incorporation, and whether the firm is a Blueprinty customer.
In this post, I use Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or MLE, to fit a Poisson regression model and estimate the relationship between Blueprinty’s software and patent outcomes while controlling for observable differences across firms.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
The outcome variable in this dataset is a count: the number of patents awarded to each firm over a five-year period. Count outcomes are non-negative integers, so the Normal distribution is not an ideal modeling choice.
The Poisson distribution is a natural starting point because it models counts directly:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)
\]
where:

\(Y_i\) is the observed patent count
\(\lambda\) is the expected number of patents

The Poisson probability mass function is:
\[
f(Y_i|\lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
Assuming the observations are independent and identically distributed, the joint likelihood is:
\[
L(\lambda | Y) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
\]
Taking logs gives the log-likelihood:
\[
\ell(\lambda | Y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-\lambda + Y_i\log(\lambda) - \log(Y_i!)\right]
\]
The log transformation is useful because it converts products into sums, making optimization much easier.

Coding the Log-Likelihood Function


Code
def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, y):
    if lam <= 0:
        return -np.inf

    ll = np.sum(-lam + y * np.log(lam) - gammaln(y + 1))
    return ll




Visualizing the Log-Likelihood


Code
y = blueprinty["patents"].values

lambda_grid = np.arange(0.1, 8, 0.05)
loglik_values = [poisson_loglikelihood(lam, y) for lam in lambda_grid]

sample_mean = np.mean(y)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(lambda_grid, loglik_values, linewidth=2)
plt.axvline(sample_mean, linestyle="--", label=f"Sample Mean = {sample_mean:.3f}")

plt.title("Poisson Log-Likelihood Function")
plt.xlabel(r"$\lambda$")
plt.ylabel("Log-Likelihood")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The curve reaches its highest point around the sample mean of the observed patent counts. Visually, the Maximum Likelihood Estimate is the value of \(\lambda\) that maximizes the log-likelihood function.


Solving for the MLE Analytically
Differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to \(\lambda\) gives:
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \lambda}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(
-1 + \frac{Y_i}{\lambda}
\right)
\]
Setting the derivative equal to zero:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(
-1 + \frac{Y_i}{\lambda}
\right)
= 0
\]
Solving for \(\lambda\) yields:
\[
\hat{\lambda}_{MLE} = \bar{Y}
\]
This result makes intuitive sense because the mean of a Poisson distribution is equal to \(\lambda\).


Finding the MLE Numerically


Code
def negative_poisson_loglikelihood(lam_array, y):
    lam = lam_array[0]
    return -poisson_loglikelihood(lam, y)

simple_result = minimize(
    negative_poisson_loglikelihood,
    x0=np.array([1.0]),
    args=(y,),
    bounds=[(0.001, None)]
)

mle_lambda = simple_result.x[0]

simple_mle_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Method": ["Numerical MLE", "Sample Mean"],

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression
The simple Poisson model assumes every firm has the same expected patent rate \(\lambda\). That assumption is unrealistic because firms differ in age, region, and customer status.
Poisson regression allows the expected patent rate to vary across firms:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)
\]
with:
\[
\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)
\]
We use the exponential function because patent rates must always remain positive, while the linear predictor \(X_i'\beta\) can take any real value.

The average difference between these two predicted outcomes gives an estimate of the association between being a Blueprinty customer and expected patent production, holding age and region fixed at each firm’s observed values.

The results provide evidence consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim: firms using the software appear to receive more patents, even after accounting for firm age and regional differences.
However, this analysis does not prove causality. The data are observational rather than experimental, so unobserved differences between customers and non-customers could still influence patent outcomes. For example, firms that adopt Blueprinty’s software may also have stronger innovation cultures, larger legal teams, or more aggressive research and development strategies.
Still, the evidence is broadly consistent with the claim that Blueprinty customers are more successful in receiving patents than comparable non-customers.

What Is a Time Series?


A time series is a sequence of values recorded at regular points in time — hourly, daily, monthly.
What makes it different from a normal table: order matters. Monday connects to Tuesday. Shuffling the rows destroys the information.



📅

Timestamp
When a visit, click, or campaign event happened.



📏

What Is a Time Series?


A time series is a sequence of values recorded at regular points in time — daily, monthly, hourly, or any consistent interval.
What makes it different from a normal data table: the order of rows matters. Monday is connected to Tuesday. You cannot shuffle the data without losing information.
Every time series has two parts:



📅

Timestamp When was it recorded?



📏

Value What was measured?

Concept 3 — Structural Break & Autocorrelation

A structural break is a point where the series permanently shifts its behaviour. Models trained before the break will give wrong answers after it.










Volatility nearly doubled and stayed there. Any model built on pre-COVID data now underestimates risk.

🔁 Autocorrelation — Does the Past Predict the Future?
Autocorrelation measures whether today’s value is related to yesterday’s. If yes, the series has memory — useful for forecasting.










During the shock, lag-1 is significant — one bad day predicted the next. Panic has momentum. Before and after: far less memory, more random.

text:
Concept 4 — Anomaly Detection
An anomaly is a data point so far from normal that it signals something genuinely unusual happened. We use the 3-sigma rule — the simplest detector that needs no labels, just the data’s own mean and spread.




The 3-Sigma Rule

Flag a point if its distance from the mean is more than 3 standard deviations.

Flag if: |value − mean| > 3 × std dev

In normally distributed data, only 0.3% of points fall that far out — so anything flagged is genuinely rare.






















⚡ ~9% of COVID-period days were anomalies — 30× the normal rate of 0.3%. The rule found the crisis automatically using nothing but the data’s own statistics.

When behaviour permanently changes, old models stop working. Detecting the break point is step one — then you retrain on the new regime.

If today’s value is linked to yesterday’s, the series has memory. During COVID, panic had momentum — one bad day predicted the next.




06 Simple Rules Detect Anomalies


The 3-sigma rule flagged 30× more anomalies during COVID using only mean and std dev — no labels, no complex model needed.




💡

These tools work on any data over time — temperature, hospital admissions, website traffic, energy usage. COVID and the stock market are just our learning example.
